task_row_model.query: Let A be a compact self-adjoint operator on a separable Hilbert space H with a simple eigenvalue λ0 and corresponding normalized eigenvector φ0. For a small self-adjoint bounded perturbation εB, derive the Rayleigh–Schrödinger expansion of the perturbed eigenvalue λ(ε) up to second order in ε, state the hypotheses needed for validity of the expansion, and explain how the result is modified if λ0 has multiplicity greater than one.

documents.content: For a nondegenerate eigenpair of a self-adjoint operator, the first-order correction to the eigenvalue is given by the Rayleigh quotient of the perturbation: λ(ε)=λ0+ε⟨φ0,Bφ0⟩+o(ε) as ε→0, assuming B is bounded and φ0 is normalized. This follows from projecting the perturbed eigenvalue equation onto φ0 and using orthogonality of the residual to leading order. The derivation uses only boundedness of B and isolation of λ0 in the spectrum; higher-order terms require control of the resolvent or more detailed spectral information and are not provided here.

A compact self-adjoint operator on a separable Hilbert space admits an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues accumulating only at zero. Its spectrum consists of a sequence of eigenvalues λn→0 (counting multiplicity) together with possibly 0. Eigenfunctions corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal, and spectral projections onto finite-dimensional eigenspaces are well-defined. This structure yields variational characterizations for nonzero eigenvalues via the min–max principle in the compact case, and compactness ensures discrete spectrum off 0 but does not by itself quantify perturbative expansions.

If λ0 is simple and isolated and B is bounded self-adjoint, the Rayleigh–Schrödinger expansion up to second order is λ(ε)=λ0+ε⟨φ0,Bφ0⟩+ε2 ∑_{n≠0} |⟨φn,Bφ0⟩|^2/(λ0−λn)+o(ε2), where {φn} is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of A and the sum runs over all other eigenvalues λn. Validity requires λ0 to be separated by a spectral gap from the rest of the spectrum so the resolvent (A−λ0I)^{-1} is bounded on φ0^{⊥}; boundedness of B ensures the perturbation series has the stated order. If λ0 has multiplicity m>1, one must diagonalize the m×m matrix with entries ⟨φi,Bφj⟩ on the eigenspace and then apply higher-order Schur complements; splitting is determined by eigenvalues of that restriction and subsequent second-order corrections involve coupling to orthogonal eigenspaces via analogous sums.

For non-self-adjoint perturbations the spectrum can behave sensitively and pseudospectra are a useful tool: small norm perturbations may produce large eigenvalue movements if the resolvent norm is large. The classical perturbation formulas for Hermitian or normal operators do not extend; instead one examines resolvent bounds and the condition numbers of eigenvectors. In infinite dimensions, non-normality interacts with spectral accumulation and approximate point spectrum, requiring different techniques such as numerical range estimates or bounds on the growth of the resolvent rather than Rayleigh–Schrödinger series.

Kato's perturbation theory provides a general framework: if A(ε)=A+εB with B bounded and λ0 an isolated eigenvalue of finite multiplicity, then eigenvalues and spectral projections depend analytically on ε in a neighborhood of zero. In the degenerate case, one studies the analytic eigenvalues of the finite-dimensional restriction of A(ε) to the invariant subspace; perturbation series exist but coefficients are obtained by solving finite matrix perturbation problems. This approach guarantees existence and smoothness of expansions but does not always yield explicit closed-form second-order sums unless one expands in the full orthonormal eigenbasis of A.
